body.problem: insrc has no grounded way to understand how it is deployed today or how it should be deployed as the system grows. The backend currently runs only as a single local daemon process installed by shell scripts, with all persistence embedded inside that one process and no accounting of the project's storage patterns, messaging, or service tiers. There is no discovery of the current deployment state, no mapping of what could be reused versus stood up new, and no structured way to reason about topology, connectivity, security and access controls, or scale and high-availability. Anyone attempting to run insrc beyond a single developer machine — self-hosted containers or orchestration, or a cloud target such as GCP or AWS — has no evidence-backed picture to work from, so deployment decisions are ad hoc, ungrounded, and inconsistent across environments.

nonGoals.text: Executing or automating actual deployments (provisioning infrastructure, running rollouts, mutating live clusters or cloud accounts).
nonGoals.rationale: The gap is the absence of grounded understanding and design of deployment; execution belongs to the existing k8s/cloud/ssh built-in tool domains and is a separate concern from the design capability this Epic frames.

nonGoals.text: Reintroducing direct cloud REST providers to Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini/Mistral for any part of deployment reasoning.
nonGoals.rationale: Project principle mandates cloud LLM access stays behind the local claude/codex CLI OAuth sessions; deployment design must not become a reason to bypass that.

nonGoals.text: Redesigning or replacing the existing local single-process daemon-install path.
nonGoals.rationale: The current install script works for the single-developer case; the missing piece is the ability to understand and design broader topologies, not to rework the one deployment that already exists.

nonGoals.text: Owning IDE-fork deployment concerns (VSCode workbench, insrc IDE contributions, the daemon installer that lives in the fork).
nonGoals.rationale: Those surfaces are owned by the insrc-ide repository; this repo's contract with the fork is the IPC surface only, so deployment design here is scoped to the backend.

assumptions.text: Deployment understanding is expected to be graph-grounded and evidence-backed — structured entity/relation summaries rather than raw file dumps — consistent with how the existing analyze framework produces context.

Deployment targets in scope are open-ended and may span local self-hosted (Docker/K3s) and cloud (GCP/AWS), since no target exists in-repo today and the current install covers only a single local process.
The new capability is expected to pattern-match the shape of insrc's existing framework subsystems (analyze, workflow) while remaining a distinct net-new subsystem rather than an extension of either.
Discovery and any execution surface for deployment reasoning are expected to reuse the existing k8s/cloud/ssh/http built-in tool domains rather than introduce parallel infrastructure access.
None of the three existing Epics (build stage, plan stage, progress streaming) overlap with deployment design, so this Epic starts from a clean problem space.

constraints.text: Deployment today is a single local daemon process with all persistence (LMDB/LanceDB/DuckDB) embedded in that one process; there are no service tiers, messaging brokers, or multi-node artifacts in-repo.
No Docker, K3s/K8s, or cloud (GCP/AWS) manifests exist in-repo — there is no container/orchestration/topology definition available to extend, so the design starts from bare shell-script install.

The IDE fork clones this repo into ~/.insrc/daemon/ and spawns the compiled out/daemon/index.js; the IPC contract (socket path, method names, payload shapes) is the only surface consumed across the two repos and must stay in lock-step.
The daemon owns all DB access; CLI, MCP, and the IDE workbench communicate via IPC only — any deployment topology must preserve this single-owner-of-storage rule.
Cloud LLM access must go through the local claude/codex CLI subprocesses; no direct cloud REST providers may be introduced by deployment reasoning.

The deployment-design capability must remain distinct from, but consistent with, the two existing framework subsystems (analyze and workflow) and should reuse the k8s/cloud/ssh/http built-in tool domains for discovery/execution.

stories.title: Establish deployment design as a distinct, consistent framework surface
stories.userValue: Anyone already familiar with insrc's analyze and workflow frameworks can reach deployment design through the same shape of interface, so the new capability feels native rather than bolted on.

acceptanceCriteria.given: a registered, indexed insrc repo and the existing analyze and workflow frameworks
acceptanceCriteria.when: a user invokes the deployment-design capability
acceptanceCriteria.then: it is reached through an interface consistent with those frameworks while remaining a distinct, separately-scoped subsystem

acceptanceCriteria.given: the deployment-design capability produces any understanding of deployment
acceptanceCriteria.when: it returns results to the user
acceptanceCriteria.then: the output is graph-grounded, structured entity/relation summaries rather than raw file dumps, consistent with how the analyze framework produces context

stories.title: Discover and report the current deployment state
stories.userValue: A user planning to run insrc beyond one developer machine starts from an evidence-backed picture of how the backend runs today instead of guessing.

acceptanceCriteria.when: a user requests a current-deployment discovery
acceptanceCriteria.then: they receive a structured, evidence-backed report describing that the backend runs today as a single local daemon process with persistence embedded in that one process

acceptanceCriteria.given: the discovery is characterizing how insrc runs today
acceptanceCriteria.when: it reports the project's storage patterns, service tiers, and messaging
acceptanceCriteria.then: it records the persistence present today and notes the absence of service tiers, messaging brokers, or multi-node artifacts where none exist

acceptanceCriteria.given: no container, orchestration, or cloud manifests exist in-repo
acceptanceCriteria.when: discovery reports the available deployment artifacts
acceptanceCriteria.then: it states plainly that only a local shell-script install exists and that no Docker, K3s, or cloud topology definition is present to extend

stories.title: Distinguish reusable infrastructure from net-new needs
stories.userValue: A user can see which existing tooling a broader deployment can lean on versus what must be stood up new, so design effort concentrates on the real gaps.

acceptanceCriteria.when: a user requests a reuse-versus-new inventory for a target deployment
acceptanceCriteria.then: each element of that deployment is classified as reused (already present today) or new (must be introduced), each with grounding

acceptanceCriteria.given: the inventory is identifying how deployment discovery and execution would reach infrastructure
acceptanceCriteria.then: it maps those surfaces onto the existing k8s, cloud, ssh, and http built-in tool domains rather than proposing parallel infrastructure-access paths

stories.title: Design deployment topology and connectivity for a chosen target
stories.userValue: A user targeting self-hosted containers or orchestration, or a cloud such as GCP or AWS, gets a grounded topology-and-connectivity design instead of ad hoc, inconsistent decisions.

acceptanceCriteria.given: a completed discovery and reuse inventory and a chosen deployment target
acceptanceCriteria.when: a user requests a topology design for that target
acceptanceCriteria.then: they receive a topology-and-connectivity design covering how components are placed and how they communicate for that target

acceptanceCriteria.given: the proposed topology includes storage-bearing components
acceptanceCriteria.when: the design defines which components may access persistence
acceptanceCriteria.then: it keeps a single owner of all database access, with every other component reaching storage only over the IPC surface

acceptanceCriteria.given: the daemon is spawned through the IDE-fork install contract
acceptanceCriteria.when: the topology changes where or how the daemon runs
acceptanceCriteria.then: the design preserves the IPC contract — socket path, method names, and payload shapes — unchanged across the two repos

stories.title: Design security and access controls for the deployment
stories.userValue: A user receives an access-control and security-boundary design layered onto the topology, so a broader deployment is not left implicitly open.

acceptanceCriteria.when: a user requests a security design for it
acceptanceCriteria.then: they receive access-control and security-boundary reasoning for the components and connections in that topology, including who may reach the single storage owner

acceptanceCriteria.given: the deployment reasons about cloud LLM access
acceptanceCriteria.when: the security design addresses how providers are reached and authenticated
acceptanceCriteria.then: it keeps cloud LLM access behind the local claude/codex CLI OAuth sessions and introduces no direct cloud REST provider path

stories.title: Design the scale and high-availability posture
stories.userValue: A user can reason about how the deployment scales and stays available as load and nodes grow, grounded in the reality that persistence lives inside one owning process today.

acceptanceCriteria.when: a user requests a scale-and-high-availability design
acceptanceCriteria.then: they receive reasoning on how the deployment scales and how it stays available as demand or node count grows for that topology

acceptanceCriteria.given: persistence is embedded inside a single owning process today
acceptanceCriteria.when: the high-availability design proposes redundancy or additional nodes
acceptanceCriteria.then: it accounts for the single-owner-of-storage rule rather than assuming shared multi-writer storage
